schema.id: Stable identifier. Never reused, never renamed once shipped.
schema.label: Short name shown in the UI.
schema.path: Absolute path. ~ is the home directory. %NAME% is a Windows environment variable. A * matches one path segment; a target only matches where the whole path exists, so a glob cannot widen into a parent.
schema.description: Plain sentence: what it is, and what happens after it is gone.
schema.risk: safe = regenerated without asking, holds nothing a person authored. caution = holds user data, or costs real time or bandwidth to rebuild.
schema.defaultEnabled: Always false. Nothing is pre-selected: cleanup is something a person chooses, never something they find already chosen for them. The field is kept rather than dropped so the loader has an invariant to enforce and a reviewer has something to notice if it ever changes.
schema.requiresAppClosed: Applications that must not be running. Empty when none apply.
schema.requiresAdmin: Needs rights DiskWatch does not ask for. Present only when true.
schema.minAgeDays: Only files last modified more than this many days ago are eligible. Present only when the entry is age-filtered.
schema.method: Always "trash", or absent, which means the same: hand the path to the trash package. Nothing in this app deletes permanently, so there is no other value. The field is kept only so the loader has something to reject — "emptyTrash" was a real value for one phase and is now a hard error.
schema.exclude: Paths under this target that must never be touched, even when the glob matches them.
schema.note: Something the implementer has to know that the user-facing description should not carry.
schema.expand: Expansion contract. When present, the target is NOT selectable as a single unit — the UI must resolve it into the listed items first, and each is chosen separately. wholeTargetSelectable is always false here; that is the point of the field. ifUnsupported says what to do when phase 2 cannot implement it, and "omit" means the entry does not ship at all rather than degrading to a folder-level checkbox.

targets.label: Application caches
targets.description: Copies apps keep so they do not have to redo work they have already done. Each app builds its own again as it runs, so the first time you open an app after this it will be a little slower.
targets.note: The JetBrains exclusion is not caution, it is a verified landmine: ~/Library/Caches/JetBrains/<product>/LocalHistory is PyCharm and IntelliJ Local History — per-file edit history, which is exactly what someone reaches for when they did not commit. It is user-authored work filed under Caches. pip and Homebrew are excluded only because they are listed separately below; without that they would be counted and deleted twice.

targets.label: Xcode DerivedData
targets.description: Files Xcode made while building your projects. Xcode rebuilds them automatically — your next build just takes longer.

targets.label: iOS Simulator caches
targets.description: Files Xcode prepared so the iPhone and iPad simulators start faster. Xcode makes them again the next time you run a simulator, and the simulators themselves stay exactly as they are.
targets.note: Caches only. CoreSimulator/Devices is excluded on purpose — it holds the simulators themselves and every app and file installed on them, which is state a developer can lose work in. Profiles/Runtimes is also excluded: re-downloadable, but multi-gigabyte downloads over someone else's connection is not a saving we get to make for them.

targets.label: npm cache
targets.description: Copies of code packages npm saved so it would not have to download the same ones twice. npm downloads whatever it needs again the next time you install something, which takes an internet connection.

targets.label: pip cache
targets.description: Copies of Python packages pip saved so it would not have to download the same ones twice. pip downloads whatever it needs again the next time you install something, which takes an internet connection.

targets.label: Cargo registry cache
targets.description: Copies of Rust code libraries Cargo downloaded for your projects. Cargo downloads them again the next time a build needs them, which takes an internet connection.
targets.note: The downloaded .crate archives only. registry/src holds the extracted sources and is left alone: Cargo rebuilds it from these archives, and deleting both makes every project rebuild from the network instead of from disk.

targets.label: Homebrew cache
targets.description: Installer files Homebrew downloaded to set up your software and does not need again. Homebrew downloads a fresh copy if you ever reinstall or update that software.

targets.label: iPhone and iPad backups
targets.description: Complete copies of your iPhone or iPad, kept on this Mac. This is what you would restore from if a device were lost, broken, or replaced, and nothing makes it again for you.
targets.note: Irreplaceable user data: this is the copy someone restores from when a device is lost or replaced. The expand contract above is a requirement, not advice. Each subfolder is one device backup keyed by device id. Offering the folder as a single checkbox is forbidden, and if the per-device listing cannot be built, ifUnsupported=omit means this entry does not ship.

targets.label: Downloads older than 90 days
targets.description: Files you downloaded more than 90 days ago and have not opened since. These are your own files rather than copies of something else — nothing downloads them again for you.
targets.note: Age-filtered per file, never the folder. Use the later of modification and last-access time: an installer kept deliberately and opened last week must not read as 90 days old because it was downloaded a year ago.

targets.label: Temporary files
targets.description: Scratch files programs write while they work and are meant to tidy up afterwards. Programs make new ones whenever they need them, and anything open right now is left alone.
targets.note: Files held open by a running process are locked and will fail to move. Expect per-file failures as normal and report them as skipped, not as an error. An installer mid-run keeps its working state here, which is a second reason a locked file must never be forced.

targets.label: Google Chrome cache
targets.description: Copies of pages and pictures Chrome saved so sites load faster when you go back to them. Chrome builds them up again as you browse, and you stay signed in to your sites.
targets.note: The glob covers every profile — Default, Profile 1 and so on — and matches only directories that actually contain a Cache subfolder, so it cannot widen into User Data itself. Cache only: Cookies, Login Data and Local Storage are sessions and saved passwords and are never touched.

targets.label: Microsoft Edge cache
targets.description: Copies of pages and pictures Edge saved so sites load faster when you go back to them. Edge builds them up again as you browse, and you stay signed in to your sites.

targets.label: Firefox cache
targets.description: Copies of pages and pictures Firefox saved so sites load faster when you go back to them. Firefox builds them up again as you browse, and you stay signed in to your sites.
targets.note: Firefox splits its profile: the cache is under LOCALAPPDATA, while the profile that holds history and logins is under APPDATA. Only the LOCALAPPDATA side is listed here, which is why this path cannot reach anything a person would miss.

targets.label: npm cache
targets.description: Copies of code packages npm saved so it would not have to download the same ones twice. npm downloads whatever it needs again the next time you install something, which takes an internet connection.
targets.note: npm's default location on Windows. A machine with a cache= line in .npmrc keeps it elsewhere and this path will simply be absent, which is the correct outcome — do not go looking for the configured one.

targets.label: pip cache
targets.description: Copies of Python packages pip saved so it would not have to download the same ones twice. pip downloads whatever it needs again the next time you install something, which takes an internet connection.

targets.label: Cargo registry cache
targets.description: Copies of Rust code libraries Cargo downloaded for your projects. Cargo downloads them again the next time a build needs them, which takes an internet connection.

targets.label: Downloads older than 90 days
targets.description: Files you downloaded more than 90 days ago and have not opened since. These are your own files rather than copies of something else — nothing downloads them again for you.
targets.note: Age-filtered per file, never the folder. Same rule as macOS: use the later of modification and last-access time.

excluded.reason: Emptying the Trash was carved out of the no-permanent-deletion rule for one phase, and then removed. Reading ~/.Trash at all needs Full Disk Access, and this app asks for no permission anywhere else — the security audit degrades a check to unknown rather than prompting. Requesting the broadest permission macOS has, in order to enable the single irreversible operation in the product, is backwards. Finder already offers Empty Trash where people expect to find it. Do not re-propose it: the rule it needed an exception to is now absolute.

Dropped together with ~/.Trash. It carried no permission cost of its own — it existed only as the Windows half of the same exception, and a rule with one carve-out in it is not the rule without one. SHEmptyRecycleBin is permanent and cannot go through the trash package, and Explorer already offers Empty Recycle Bin. Do not re-propose it on its own.

Excluded by instruction, and the reasoning holds: it is the only copy of the previous Windows install and of any user file that did not survive the upgrade. Windows removes it on its own after ten days. Deleting it wrongly is unrecoverable, and it needs handling this list cannot express.

Needs administrator rights, which DiskWatch does not ask for anywhere. It would fail on every non-elevated run, which is most of them. Revisit only if the app ever gains an elevation story — and the security audit deliberately does not have one. Confirmed excluded: two cache folders do not justify building an elevation story the app has avoided everywhere else.

Needs administrator rights, and doing it correctly means stopping the Windows Update service first. Stopping a service is a system change, not a deletion, and it is outside what a disk cleaner should do. Clearing it during an update leaves Windows Update needing a repair. Confirmed excluded: two cache folders do not justify building an elevation story the app has avoided everywhere else.
Holds the simulators themselves and every app and file installed on them. Recreating a device is easy; recovering what was inside one is not.
Contains LocalHistory, which is PyCharm and IntelliJ per-file edit history — user-authored work that happens to be filed under Caches. Verified present on the development machine.
Per-volume bins on external and network drives. DiskWatch has no way to know whose drive it is or what else uses it.
Not researched. Mostly noise, but crash reports here are sometimes the only record of why something failed, and the saving is small.
